# Process cooling water cleaning, flushing and passivation — Tull Creek Data Hall, turnover package

You are the commissioning engineer for the flushing contractor on a new data hall. The project
document library for this task is the directory tree around this file: `drawings/` (P&ID and
isometric sheets, site logistics and the temporary power single line, DXF, plan units are feet),
`schedules/` (pipe, equipment, valve and tie-in schedules, XLSX), `specs/` (the project
specification sections, DOCX), `standards/` (the public standards and criteria documents the
specification adopts, PDF), `site/` (construction water, the water analysis, the discharge
authorisation and temporary power, DOCX / PDF / XLSX), `vendor_data/` (reviewed submittals and a
priced chemical quotation, PDF / XLSX), `commissioning/` (turnover milestones, the hydrostatic test
record and a checklist template, XLSX / CSV) and `correspondence/` (RFI responses). Not every
document is relevant, and the information you need is spread across them: read the project
specification first and let it tell you which documents govern what.

Some documents in the library are **scanned images with no text layer**. Their contents cannot be
extracted as text and must be read as images; do not conclude that a document is empty or
irrelevant because text extraction returns nothing.

## Situation

The Process Cooling Water (PCW) loop is mechanically complete. It is divided into eight
tie-in-bounded circuits of different sizes, metallurgies and hold-up volumes. Before turnover every
circuit must be flushed, chemically cleaned, rinsed, passivated and filled with its treatment
programme, and the whole campaign must be executed with a fixed rented fleet of flush skids, a
metered construction-water allocation, a single authorised sewer discharge point, the temporary
power available at each tie-in, two commissioning crews and a contractual turnover date.

Which lines belong to which circuit is shown on the drawings, not tabulated anywhere. The rest of
the engineering is yours: the flow each circuit must be flushed at and whether the skid you assign
can deliver it against that circuit's head; the treatment programme each circuit's metallurgy and
the site's makeup water admit; how much product that needs and how long the passivation film must be
held; how many rinse displacements it takes to reach the acceptance criterion; whether rinse water
can be cascaded from one circuit to another; where each discharge goes; and how all of that fits the
water, fleet, power, discharge and schedule limits at the lowest total programme cost.

## Deliverable

Produce `output/submission.zip` containing the seven files below. **The schema is a contract, not
part of the problem: every column and every stage token you need is listed here.** Column names are
matched case-insensitively and `_`, `-` and space are equivalent; common synonyms are accepted, and
extra columns of your own are ignored. Rows may be in any order. Use these stage tokens:

    HYDRO   INITIAL_FLUSH   CHEM_CLEAN   DRAIN_RINSE   PASSIVATE   HOLD   FINAL_FILL

You may add activities of your own (set-up, strainer removal, demobilisation); they are ignored, not
penalised. A stage token that cannot be resolved costs the package family; and if the stage it was
meant to be was one of the seven above, the circuit also loses every family that needed that stage —
an unreadable token does not stand in for the stage it was meant to name.

One cell value is fatal, and only in one place. In the numeric columns the grader reads — `flow_gpm`,
`velocity_fps`, `reynolds`, `required_head_ft`, `skid_head_avail_ft`, `duration_h`,
`circuit_volume_gal`, `system_volume_gal`, `passes`, `water_volume_gal`, `discharge_volume_gal`,
`discharge_ph`, `discharge_temp_f`, `target_ppm`, `product_quantity`, `basis_volume_gal`,
`ph_target_lo`, `ph_target_hi`, `threshold_value`, `start_h`, `finish_h` — a cell reading `TBD`,
`TBA`, `to be determined`, `to be advised`, `NaN`, `Inf`, `XXX` or `<fill in>` scores the whole
package zero: a placeholder
is not an answer — in any of the four plan CSVs, on any row. In any other column, including every
column of your own, those words are ignored. `--`, `N/A`, `NONE` and an empty cell are ordinary
"not applicable" everywhere and are never penalised, so a column a row does not use (the skid and
flow columns on `HYDRO` and `HOLD`, the test pressure off the hydrostatic row) should be left blank
or set to one of those rather than to `TBD`.

The rented fleet is a closed vocabulary: `skid_id` on a pumped row must name one or more of the
three units on hire, `+`-joined. Case, spaces, hyphens and underscores are equivalent. A cell that
names anything else — a model rather than a unit, a unit that was never hired, or nothing at all —
costs the skid-fleet family for the programme; it never makes the package unreadable.

`HYDRO` and `HOLD` are not pumped stages: on those rows the skid, flow, velocity, Reynolds and head
columns do not apply and may be left blank or set to `NONE`. `HYDRO` carries its test pressure and
its duration; `HOLD` carries only its duration. Every other stage carries the full row. A circuit
whose hydrostatic test is already on record as accepted needs no `HYDRO` row; if you file one for
it, give it a duration of zero and no water, and it is read as a test not performed.

1. `flush_plan.csv` — one row per circuit and stage. Columns:
   `circuit_id` · `stage` · `skid_id` (the rented unit ids, `+`-joined if more than one) ·
   `skids_parallel` (count) · `flow_gpm` · `governing_segment` (line number) ·
   `governing_id_in` (in.) · `velocity_fps` (ft/s) · `reynolds` · `required_head_ft` (ft w.c.) ·
   `skid_head_avail_ft` (ft w.c.) · `duration_h` (the scheduled occupancy, hours) ·
   `circuit_volume_gal` (the FLUSH volume) · `system_volume_gal` · `passes` (displacements, on the
   flush and rinse rows) · `water_source` (`MAKEUP`, or `CASCADE_FROM:<circuit>`) ·
   `water_volume_gal` · `discharge_route` (`SEWER`, `HAUL` or `NONE`) · `discharge_volume_gal` ·
   `discharge_ph` · `discharge_temp_f` (degF) · `test_pressure_psig` (on the hydrostatic row) ·
   `protection` (the temporary bypasses and strainer fitted for that stage) ·
   `turnover_method` (the method the project specification permits at turnover).
2. `chemistry_plan.csv` — one row per circuit, stage and product. Columns:
   `circuit_id` · `stage` · `program` (the treatment programme, on the treatment rows) ·
   `product_id` · `active_species` · `target_ppm` · `basis_volume_gal` (the volume the dose is
   referred to) · `product_quantity` · `product_unit` · `packages` (whole packages) ·
   `ph_target_lo` · `ph_target_hi` · `hold_days` · `source_doc` · `source_clause`.
   A roll-up row whose stage is an order total is ignored.
3. `acceptance_matrix.csv` — one row per circuit, gate and parameter. Columns:
   `circuit_id` · `gate` · `parameter` · `method` · `sample_point_tag` ·
   `threshold_op` (`>=`/`<=`, or `lower limit`/`upper limit`) · `threshold_value` · `units` ·
   `basis_doc` · `basis_clause`. The gates and parameters the turnover log must carry are listed in
   the project specification; the grader matches a row by its gate and the quantity named in its
   parameter, not by an exact spelling.
4. `schedule.csv` — one row per activity; a stage may be split into several. Columns:
   `activity_id` · `circuit_id` · `stage` · `predecessor_ids` · `start_h` · `finish_h` (hours from
   mobilisation) · `skid_id` · `crew_id` · `water_draw_gal`.
5. `resources.json` — an object with `skid_assignment`, `water_profile`, `discharge_profile`,
   `power_check`, `chemical_orders` and `cost`. `chemical_orders` is a list of objects carrying at
   least `product_id`, `packages`, `lead_days` and `order_by_day` (days from mobilisation; negative
   means before it). `cost` carries the breakdown and a total under `total_usd`.
6. `constraint_register.csv` — columns `id, document, clause, requirement, value, items_bound`:
   every requirement you applied, each with the document and clause or table it comes from, the
   value you used and what it binds. Cite the real project documents and clauses, not this brief.
   The register is scored on recall of the requirements the grader checks (at least 90 % of the hard
   requirements must be present, matched on document plus clause) and on value agreement; extra
   correct rows are neutral and there is no cap on the number of rows, and **a hard requirement
   missing from the register makes every family it governs count as not passed**. Rows citing a
   superseded, cancelled or non-adopted document as their authority count against you: **a single
   such row fails the register family**. Recording that a document is superseded while citing the
   current one, or citing a standard an adopted document itself invokes, is not such a row.
   **The register lists only the requirements you applied.** A row whose `document` cell names a
   superseded, cancelled or non-adopted document is a row citing that document as its authority
   **whatever its requirement or value text says** — writing "out of scope", "not applied" or
   "reviewed and rejected" in another column does not make it a different row. Record the documents
   you read and rejected, and why, in `MOP.md`, not in the register.
7. `MOP.md` — the Method of Procedure: the execution narrative **and** the design basis. The design
   basis must give, for each circuit, **the governing constraint and its margin**. The governing
   constraint is whichever of these five your own plan leaves the least room against — the flushing
   duty against the head the assigned skid can deliver; the rinse endpoint; the authorised programme
   discharge volume; the site's daily water allocation; the temporary power available at the tie-in
   — and the margin is the fractional room left, `(limit − achieved) / limit`, as a decimal. Name
   one per circuit and state its margin. Some of these margins can be written in more than one
   quantity — the rinse in displacements or in the quantity its endpoint is measured in — and they
   are genuinely different numbers; **every form the project specification permits counts, and which
   constraint binds is decided using whichever permitted form of each is the tighter**, so a
   constraint that is tightest in any permitted quantity is a defensible answer. The rinse margin may be
   given either in displacements or in whatever quantity the acceptance
   criterion you are working to is expressed in. Which one binds, and by how much, is yours to
   work out; record the resolution of every conflict you found between the
   project documents, the margins and judgement calls you made, the defects you found, and a safety
   section discharging the chemical-handling obligations of the standard the specification adopts
   for hazard communication.

Every number you report must agree with the plan it describes: the figures that are scored are
recomputed from your flows, passes, routes, methods and schedule, not taken from your columns.
The rinse is the one exception for the effluent columns: its effluent runs from the spent
cleaning solution to the makeup water over the displacements, so any `discharge_ph` and
`discharge_temp_f` inside the acceptance band the discharge authorisation states is accepted on
a `DRAIN_RINSE` row.

The project specification states how water, effluent, attended time and cost are accounted, and what
the turnover options are. Follow it: the plan is priced on that basis.

## How the package is assessed

The plan is checked circuit by circuit against the requirements of the project documents, and the
programme is credited for its total cost against the lowest cost the documents allow: a cheaper
programme scores higher. Each circuit scores 0.4·p + 0.6·[h = 1]·O, where p is the fraction of its 24
constraint families that count, h the fraction of its 20 hard families that count (a family counts
when the circuit passes it and the register carries the hard requirements that govern it; [h = 1] is
1 when all 20 count, else 0), and O is the lowest cost the documents allow divided by the cost of your
programme, at most 1. A hard failure withholds O. The task score is the mean over the graded circuits.
A circuit whose rows are missing or unparseable scores 0.

Work from the documents. Where they leave something to the engineer, decide and record it in the
design basis.

SECTION 23 25 16 - PROCESS COOLING WATER CLEANING, FLUSHING AND PASSIVATION
Tull Creek Data Hall - Issued for Construction, Rev 3, 2026-07-14
1.1   SUMMARY
This Section covers pre-operational cleaning, flushing, chemical cleaning, passivation and turnover of the Process Cooling Water (PCW) system, circuit by circuit.
The PCW system is a closed process cooling water loop. Apply the closed-system provisions of the governing water-treatment criteria document; the provisions written for open recirculating cooling-tower systems do not apply to this system except where this Section invokes them explicitly.
Where this Section and the governing water-treatment criteria document both address a subject, the more restrictive requirement governs.
1.2   GOVERNING DOCUMENTS
UFC 3-230-13, Industrial Water Treatment Operation and Maintenance (current edition). The 2005 edition, UFC 3-240-13FN, is cancelled and must not be used.
DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92, Thermodynamics, Heat Transfer and Fluid Flow, Volume 3, for all hydraulic relations.
40 CFR 403, General Pretreatment Regulations, for discharge to the publicly owned treatment works.
29 CFR 1910.1200, Hazard Communication, for all products brought on site.
Section 23 21 16 for pipe materials, roughness and the hydrostatic test regime.
1.5   FLUSHING, TESTING AND WATER-TREATMENT LOG
Maintain and submit a log recording, for every circuit: the minimum flushing velocity achieved and the segment at which it was measured; the temporary strainer mesh and its removal milestone; the chemical cleaning circulation time; the rinse water test results (clarity, suspended solids, conductivity and pH) against the makeup water; the passivation inhibitor residual, pH and film-formation hold duration; and every discharge event with its volume, route, pH and temperature. Use the form of CX-03.
Submit with the log an acceptance matrix stating, for every circuit, the acceptance threshold applied at each gate, with the document and clause it comes from. The matrix must carry at least the following, each with the sense and the numeric value of its threshold:
  a. RINSE gate: conductivity (upper limit), pH (lower limit and upper limit);
  b. PASSIVATION gate: the inhibitor residual at the start of film formation (lower limit);
  c. DISCHARGE gate: pH (lower limit) and temperature (upper limit) at the authorised discharge point;
  d. TURNOVER gate: the maintenance inhibitor residual (lower limit) and the total aerobic bacteria count (upper limit), both to the limits of the governing water-treatment criteria document.
1.6   DESIGN BASIS AND METHOD OF PROCEDURE
Submit a Method of Procedure (MOP) containing the execution narrative and the design basis.
Where a constraint can be expressed in more than one quantity - the rinse, for instance, in displacements or in conductivity - the margin may be stated in ANY of them; state which.
The design basis must state, for each circuit, a line of exactly the form
    GOVERNING CONSTRAINT <circuit>: <constraint family> (margin <value>)
where <constraint family> is the constraint family that is binding for that circuit and <value> is its relative margin, that is (limit - achieved)/limit for an upper limit and (achieved - limit)/limit for a lower limit, as a decimal fraction.
The design basis must also record the resolution of every conflict found between the project documents, the margins applied, and the defects found in the documents.
3.2   HYDRAULIC BASIS
Compute every hydraulic quantity by the relations of DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92 with the following project conventions. Design flush water properties: density 62.30 lbm/ft3, kinematic viscosity 1.08e-5 ft2/s at 68 degF.
For DOSING arithmetic - converting a target residual in parts per million to a mass of active species - use a water density of 8.34 lb/gal. A residual of 1 ppm in 1,000 gallons is therefore 0.00834 lb of the active species.
a. Velocity in a leg is v = Q_leg / A, where Q_leg is that leg's share of the circuit flow and A is the inside cross-sectional area from Schedule M-601. Parallel legs of one line carry an equal share.
b. Friction factor from the Colebrook-White relation, solved iteratively:
       1/sqrt(f) = -2 log10( (e/D)/3.7 + 2.51/(Re sqrt(f)) )
   with absolute roughness e from Section 23 21 16 and Re = v D / nu. Below Re 2000 use f = 64/Re.
c. Head loss in a run is the Darcy loss over the straight length PLUS the equivalent length of its fittings, L_eq = (sum L/D) x D, with sum L/D from Schedule M-601:
       h = f ((L + L_eq)/D) v^2 / (2 g)
d. The required head of a circulation set is the sum of: the static lift from the tie-in to the circuit high point (isometrics M-ISO-2xx); the head loss of the MAIN circulation path, that is the lines shown on M-601 with a single leg, at the total circuit flow; the pressure drop of every component left in the flushed path, scaled as dP_rated x (Q/Q_rated)^2 from Schedule M-602; and, for EACH skid separately at that skid's own share of the flow, the head loss of its temporary hose run and the pressure drop of its temporary strainer, scaled as dP_rated x (Q_skid/Q_rated)^2 from VD-05.
e. Where two or more skids are used on one circuit they are connected in parallel: they share the total flow equally and each must develop the required head at its own flow, per DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92.
f. A duty point beyond the last point of a published pump curve is not acceptable.
3.3   FLUSHING VELOCITY
The flushing flow of a circuit shall be not less than the flow required to achieve, in EVERY leg of EVERY line of that circuit, the greater of:
  a. the water velocity that the governing water-treatment criteria document requires for keeping foulants in suspension; and
  b. the project minimum for the circuit's velocity class, namely 4.0 ft/s for any circuit that serves a plate heat exchanger or a cold-plate device, and 2.0 ft/s otherwise.
The flushing flow shall be maintained through the initial flush, the chemical cleaning circulation and every rinse displacement.
NUMBER OF INITIAL FLUSH DISPLACEMENTS. Not fewer than ONE full circuit displacement before the cleaning charge is made up. More may be used where the Contractor judges the construction debris warrants it; the water, effluent and attended time of every displacement declared are accounted under cl.3.9 and cl.3.10 and are the Contractor's cost.
Record in the log the segment at which the velocity is lowest; that segment is the governing segment of the circuit.
3.4   CHEMICAL CLEANING
Clean each circuit with the cleaning product scheduled for its metallurgy in VD-06, at the application rate stated there, referred to the SYSTEM volume of the circuit (pipework plus the hold-up of every component of the circuit, whether or not it is bypassed for flushing).
The cleaning product is dosed on that VOLUMETRIC application rate, not to a target residual: state the basis volume and the quantity of product, and leave the target residual not applicable on a cleaning row (VD-06 Note 4a).
Carry the polymer dispersant of the governing water-treatment criteria document with the cleaning charge, at the active dosage that document states for keeping foulants in suspension.
Circulate the cleaning solution for not less than the circulation time the governing water-treatment criteria document requires, then drain, flush and clean all strainers.
That circulation time is CONTACT TIME and is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS: it is the sum of the hours of the activities scheduled for the stage, and an idle gap between two of them is not contact time (cl.3.10 b).
Protect every component listed in M-602 as having a temporary bypass provision by fitting that bypass for the initial flush and the chemical cleaning. A component left in the flushed path must be shown to be within the maximum allowable pressure drop, the maximum temperature and the maximum particle size that M-602 gives it, at the declared flow.
3.5   PASSIVATION AND TREATMENT PROGRAM
Select the closed-system treatment program from the governing water-treatment criteria document for the circuit's metallurgy and for the makeup water analysis SW-02, and maintain the residual and pH that document specifies for the program selected.
Where that document's programme SELECTION TABLE and the controlling paragraph text of the individual programmes differ as to which programme suits a metallurgy, the paragraph text of the programme governs. The selection table is organised by system type, not by metallurgy, and does not restrict a programme to the system types it happens to list.
Where that document tabulates a quantity in more than one table, the tables it identifies for PASSIVATION govern for passivation dosages, pH bands and film-formation times; a table written for a different duty does not.
Passivate with the inhibitor technology that document tabulates for passivation, at a residual inside the tabulated dosage band and a pH inside the tabulated pH band, and hold the film-formation period that the CURRENT edition of that document tabulates.
That hold, like every other required period of this Section, is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS (cl.3.10 b).
Dose all treatment chemicals on the SYSTEM volume of the circuit.
Where copper is wetted anywhere in the circuit, carry the azole at not less than the residual the governing document requires.
3.6   RINSE DISPLACEMENT MODEL
The number of rinse displacements required after chemical cleaning shall be computed from the project displacement model:
       C_n = C_mk + (C_0 - C_mk) exp(-eta n)
where C_n is the circuit water conductivity after n full circuit-volume displacements, C_mk is the makeup water conductivity from SW-02, C_0 is the conductivity of the spent cleaning solution from VD-06, n is the number of displacements of the circuit FLUSH volume (pipework plus the hold-up of components that are NOT bypassed), and eta is the mixing efficiency of the circuit:
       eta = 0.45 for a circuit that contains a parallel cold-plate manifold bank or coil bank, that is, a circuit any of whose components Schedule M-602 describes as a cold-plate manifold bank or a coil bank
       eta = 0.62 for every other circuit
n shall be a whole number of displacements, and shall be large enough that C_n satisfies the rinse acceptance criterion of the governing water-treatment criteria document.
That criterion states the rinse pH as a tolerance and as a window in one sentence. BOTH readings are acceptable to this project: a pH limit filed either as the tolerance about the makeup pH of SW-02 or as the absolute window the document names satisfies cl.1.5, and a control band inside their intersection satisfies both.
Each displacement takes the time the declared flow needs to move the circuit FLUSH volume, and that time too is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS (cl.3.10 b).
A displacement may be made with the final rinse effluent of another circuit that has already satisfied the rinse acceptance criterion (a cascade). A cascaded displacement counts as a full displacement. No circuit may receive more than one cascaded displacement, and the donor circuit's rinse must be complete before the cascade begins.
3.7   DISCHARGE
All flush, cleaning and rinse effluent shall be discharged to the metered sanitary sewer connection authorised in SW-03, or removed from site by tanker to a permitted disposal facility, at the rates quoted in SW-01 and RFI-031.
Effluent shall meet the general pretreatment prohibitions of 40 CFR 403 and the local limits of SW-03. Any effluent stream containing a constituent for which SW-03 states a local limit that the stream cannot meet shall be hauled off site.
The programme total authorised at the metered connection shall not be exceeded.
3.8   TURNOVER
Bring each circuit to the maintenance residual and pH of the selected treatment program by ONE of the two methods below, at the Contractor's option. Declare the method used for each circuit in the plan, as turnover_method. Then recirculate for not less than the period the governing water-treatment criteria document requires before sampling, and sample while circulating.
  RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP - the passivation charge is retained in the circuit and the circuit is topped up to its SYSTEM volume with treated makeup water carrying the maintenance charge. Permitted only where the maintenance residual of the selected program is not below its passivation residual, so that the top-up raises rather than dilutes the inhibitor level.
  DRAIN_AND_REFILL - the passivation charge is drained to the route declared for it and the circuit is refilled to its SYSTEM volume with treated makeup water carrying the maintenance charge.
REPORTING CONVENTION. On every chemistry row, target_ppm is the ABSOLUTE residual the circuit is to be held at, and product_quantity is the quantity the dose ADDS. Under RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP those differ: the top-up adds only the difference between the maintenance residual and the residual the retained charge already carries. Either the absolute quantity or the increment is accepted, provided the basis volume is stated.
Where two tabulated inhibitors are carried at once - an inhibitor and a copper azole, for instance - and their tabulated pH bands overlap only in part, control to the INTERSECTION of the two bands, which satisfies both.
3.9   WATER AND EFFLUENT ACCOUNTING
Account the water drawn and the effluent produced by each circuit as follows, where V_f is the circuit FLUSH volume, V_s its SYSTEM volume, n_f the number of initial flush displacements, n_r the number of rinse displacements and c is 1 if one displacement is cascaded in and 0 otherwise. State both figures for every stage in the plan.
    hydrostatic test (where one is owed)   draw V_f              effluent V_f
    initial flush                          draw n_f x V_f        effluent n_f x V_f
    chemical cleaning                      draw V_f              effluent V_f
    rinse                                  draw (n_r - c) x V_f  effluent (n_r - 1) x V_f - d
    passivation charge                     draw 0                effluent 0
    film-formation hold                    draw 0                effluent 0
    turnover, RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP            draw V_s - V_f        effluent 0
    turnover, DRAIN_AND_REFILL             draw V_s              effluent V_f
The circuit is left FULL at the end of the last rinse displacement, so that displacement is not drained: that is why the rinse effluent is one displacement less than the rinse draw.
The passivation charge is dosed into the water standing in the circuit at the end of the rinse; it is not a fresh fill.
A rinse that takes one cascaded displacement and draws the rest from the metered supply is a single row with a single water_source: declare it CASCADE_FROM:<donor circuit>. The makeup balance above already accounts for the other displacements being drawn fresh.
d is the volume this circuit DONATES to a cascade: a cascade transfers exactly one receiver displacement volume, that is the FLUSH volume of the receiving circuit, out of the donor's final rinse effluent, so the donor's effluent falls by that volume and the receiver's draw falls by the same volume. A circuit may donate to at most one receiver and receive from at most one donor, and a donor's FLUSH volume must be not less than its receiver's, or it cannot fill it.
These figures balance: over the programme, water drawn equals effluent produced plus the SYSTEM volume left standing in every circuit at turnover.
Water drawn by an activity that spans midnight is counted against each calendar day in proportion to the hours of the activity in that day (SW-01 cl.2).
3.10   COST BASIS
Price the programme on the following basis, and report the total and its breakdown in the plan.
  a. Skid rental: the fleet is on HIRE TO THE PROGRAMME, not to a circuit. Each rented unit is charged ONE day rate (SW-01 cl.3, VD-01, VD-02) for every CALENDAR DAY on which it is held anywhere on the works, counted ONCE however many circuits it serves that day. A calendar day is the period [24k, 24k+24) hours from mobilisation, k = 0, 1, 2 ... A unit is held on a day if any scheduled activity that declares it overlaps that day; a unit released for the film-formation hold is not held during it. APPORTIONMENT: divide each unit-day between the circuits that held that unit that day IN PROPORTION TO THE HOURS each held it inside the day, merging any overlap within a circuit. The share so obtained is a real number and is NOT rounded; the whole day is charged once and divided. Two circuits that share a unit-day therefore pay a part each, and a circuit whose work is spread thinly across many days pays for every one of them.
  b. Commissioning crew: a crew is ENGAGED BY THE SHIFT, not by the circuit. Each crew is charged ONE shift rate for every 12-hour SHIFT [12k, 12k+12) hours from mobilisation in which it attends anything at all, counted ONCE however many circuits it attends in it. APPORTIONMENT: divide each crew-shift between the circuits attended in it IN PROPORTION TO THE ATTENDED HOURS each took inside the shift; the share is a real number and is NOT rounded. A stage's attended hours are spread over the shifts its scheduled activities occupy IN PROPORTION TO THE HOURS of those activities in each shift, the same convention cl.3.9 uses for the daily water draw.
     DURATION IS OCCUPIED TIME. A stage lasts as long as its activities OCCUPY: its duration is the SUM of the hours of the activities scheduled for it, and an idle gap between two of them is no part of it. No period this Section requires - a contact time, a circulation time, a displacement at the declared flow, a recirculation, a film-formation hold - is satisfied by an ENVELOPE that merely contains it. Work not done in the gap is not work done. The attended time of a stage is:
       hydrostatic test        the specified hold
       initial flush           n_f x V_f at the declared flow
       chemical cleaning       the greater of the required circulation time and V_f at the declared flow
       rinse                   n_r x V_f at the declared flow
       passivation charge      V_f at the declared flow, plus the required recirculation
       turnover                the fill volume of the declared method at the declared flow, plus the required recirculation
     An unattended film-formation hold, and unattended standby inside a longer scheduled occupancy, are not charged (SW-01 cl.3, 01 91 13 cl.1.7); a stage with no attended time opens no shift. A crew attends one activity at a time and a rented unit serves one circuit at a time, so no crew may be charged with more than 12 attended hours in a shift and no unit held for more than 24 hours in a day.
     WHAT a AND b MEAN FOR THE PROGRAMME. Both lines are bought by the period, so the two of them price the SEQUENCE, not the circuit: a programme that dovetails its circuits into the same unit-days and the same crew-shifts pays a fraction of what the same engineering costs when the circuits are run one after another. Neither line can be worked out from one circuit in isolation, and a circuit's share of both moves when another circuit's schedule moves. Against that pull stands cl.3.9 and SW-01 cl.2: the site's daily water allocation is shared too, so drawing the whole programme into a few days buys the excess at the trucked rate, and the cascade links of cl.3.6 force the circuits they join to rinse in sequence. The economic plan is the one that settles those against each other.
  c. Water: metered rate up to the daily allocation and the trucked rate above it (SW-01 cl.1, cl.2). APPORTIONMENT: the allocation is a site-wide meter, so form ONE programme-wide average rate - the metered and trucked volumes priced at their own rates, divided by the total volume drawn - and apply that single rate to every circuit's draw. Do not attempt to attribute particular gallons to particular circuits.
  d. Effluent: the sewer rate for volume to the metered connection, the tanker rate for volume remove

SECTION 23 25 16 - PROCESS COOLING WATER CLEANING, FLUSHING AND PASSIVATION
Tull Creek Data Hall - Issued for Construction, Rev 3, 2026-07-14
1.1   SUMMARY
This Section covers pre-operational cleaning, flushing, chemical cleaning, passivation and turnover of the Process Cooling Water (PCW) system, circuit by circuit.
The PCW system is a closed process cooling water loop. Apply the closed-system provisions of the governing water-treatment criteria document; the provisions written for open recirculating cooling-tower systems do not apply to this system except where this Section invokes them explicitly.
Where this Section and the governing water-treatment criteria document both address a subject, the more restrictive requirement governs.
1.2   GOVERNING DOCUMENTS
UFC 3-230-13, Industrial Water Treatment Operation and Maintenance (current edition). The 2005 edition, UFC 3-240-13FN, is cancelled and must not be used.
DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92, Thermodynamics, Heat Transfer and Fluid Flow, Volume 3, for all hydraulic relations.
40 CFR 403, General Pretreatment Regulations, for discharge to the publicly owned treatment works.
29 CFR 1910.1200, Hazard Communication, for all products brought on site.
Section 23 21 16 for pipe materials, roughness and the hydrostatic test regime.
1.5   FLUSHING, TESTING AND WATER-TREATMENT LOG
Maintain and submit a log recording, for every circuit: the minimum flushing velocity achieved and the segment at which it was measured; the temporary strainer mesh and its removal milestone; the chemical cleaning circulation time; the rinse water test results (clarity, suspended solids, conductivity and pH) against the makeup water; the passivation inhibitor residual, pH and film-formation hold duration; and every discharge event with its volume, route, pH and temperature. Use the form of CX-03.
Submit with the log an acceptance matrix stating, for every circuit, the acceptance threshold applied at each gate, with the document and clause it comes from. The matrix must carry at least the following, each with the sense and the numeric value of its threshold:
  a. RINSE gate: conductivity (upper limit), pH (lower limit and upper limit);
  b. PASSIVATION gate: the inhibitor residual at the start of film formation (lower limit);
  c. DISCHARGE gate: pH (lower limit) and temperature (upper limit) at the authorised discharge point;
  d. TURNOVER gate: the maintenance inhibitor residual (lower limit) and the total aerobic bacteria count (upper limit), both to the limits of the governing water-treatment criteria document.
1.6   DESIGN BASIS AND METHOD OF PROCEDURE
Submit a Method of Procedure (MOP) containing the execution narrative and the design basis.
Where a constraint can be expressed in more than one quantity - the rinse, for instance, in displacements or in conductivity - the margin may be stated in ANY of them; state which.
The design basis must state, for each circuit, a line of exactly the form
    GOVERNING CONSTRAINT <circuit>: <constraint family> (margin <value>)
where <constraint family> is the constraint family that is binding for that circuit and <value> is its relative margin, that is (limit - achieved)/limit for an upper limit and (achieved - limit)/limit for a lower limit, as a decimal fraction.
The design basis must also record the resolution of every conflict found between the project documents, the margins applied, and the defects found in the documents.
3.2   HYDRAULIC BASIS
Compute every hydraulic quantity by the relations of DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92 with the following project conventions. Design flush water properties: density 62.30 lbm/ft3, kinematic viscosity 1.08e-5 ft2/s at 68 degF.
For DOSING arithmetic - converting a target residual in parts per million to a mass of active species - use a water density of 8.34 lb/gal. A residual of 1 ppm in 1,000 gallons is therefore 0.00834 lb of the active species.
a. Velocity in a leg is v = Q_leg / A, where Q_leg is that leg's share of the circuit flow and A is the inside cross-sectional area from Schedule M-601. Parallel legs of one line carry an equal share.
b. Friction factor from the Colebrook-White relation, solved iteratively:
       1/sqrt(f) = -2 log10( (e/D)/3.7 + 2.51/(Re sqrt(f)) )
   with absolute roughness e from Section 23 21 16 and Re = v D / nu. Below Re 2000 use f = 64/Re.
c. Head loss in a run is the Darcy loss over the straight length PLUS the equivalent length of its fittings, L_eq = (sum L/D) x D, with sum L/D from Schedule M-601:
       h = f ((L + L_eq)/D) v^2 / (2 g)
d. The required head of a circulation set is the sum of: the static lift from the tie-in to the circuit high point (isometrics M-ISO-2xx); the head loss of the MAIN circulation path, that is the lines shown on M-601 with a single leg, at the total circuit flow; the pressure drop of every component left in the flushed path, scaled as dP_rated x (Q/Q_rated)^2 from Schedule M-602; and, for EACH skid separately at that skid's own share of the flow, the head loss of its temporary hose run and the pressure drop of its temporary strainer, scaled as dP_rated x (Q_skid/Q_rated)^2 from VD-05.
e. Where two or more skids are used on one circuit they are connected in parallel: they share the total flow equally and each must develop the required head at its own flow, per DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92.
f. A duty point beyond the last point of a published pump curve is not acceptable.
3.3   FLUSHING VELOCITY
The flushing flow of a circuit shall be not less than the flow required to achieve, in EVERY leg of EVERY line of that circuit, the greater of:
  a. the water velocity that the governing water-treatment criteria document requires for keeping foulants in suspension; and
  b. the project minimum for the circuit's velocity class, namely 4.0 ft/s for any circuit that serves a plate heat exchanger or a cold-plate device, and 2.0 ft/s otherwise.
The flushing flow shall be maintained through the initial flush, the chemical cleaning circulation and every rinse displacement.
NUMBER OF INITIAL FLUSH DISPLACEMENTS. Not fewer than ONE full circuit displacement before the cleaning charge is made up. More may be used where the Contractor judges the construction debris warrants it; the water, effluent and attended time of every displacement declared are accounted under cl.3.9 and cl.3.10 and are the Contractor's cost.
Record in the log the segment at which the velocity is lowest; that segment is the governing segment of the circuit.
3.4   CHEMICAL CLEANING
Clean each circuit with the cleaning product scheduled for its metallurgy in VD-06, at the application rate stated there, referred to the SYSTEM volume of the circuit (pipework plus the hold-up of every component of the circuit, whether or not it is bypassed for flushing).
The cleaning product is dosed on that VOLUMETRIC application rate, not to a target residual: state the basis volume and the quantity of product, and leave the target residual not applicable on a cleaning row (VD-06 Note 4a).
Carry the polymer dispersant of the governing water-treatment criteria document with the cleaning charge, at the active dosage that document states for keeping foulants in suspension.
Circulate the cleaning solution for not less than the circulation time the governing water-treatment criteria document requires, then drain, flush and clean all strainers.
That circulation time is CONTACT TIME and is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS: it is the sum of the hours of the activities scheduled for the stage, and an idle gap between two of them is not contact time (cl.3.10 b).
Protect every component listed in M-602 as having a temporary bypass provision by fitting that bypass for the initial flush and the chemical cleaning. A component left in the flushed path must be shown to be within the maximum allowable pressure drop, the maximum temperature and the maximum particle size that M-602 gives it, at the declared flow.
3.5   PASSIVATION AND TREATMENT PROGRAM
Select the closed-system treatment program from the governing water-treatment criteria document for the circuit's metallurgy and for the makeup water analysis SW-02, and maintain the residual and pH that document specifies for the program selected.
Where that document's programme SELECTION TABLE and the controlling paragraph text of the individual programmes differ as to which programme suits a metallurgy, the paragraph text of the programme governs. The selection table is organised by system type, not by metallurgy, and does not restrict a programme to the system types it happens to list.
Where that document tabulates a quantity in more than one table, the tables it identifies for PASSIVATION govern for passivation dosages, pH bands and film-formation times; a table written for a different duty does not.
Passivate with the inhibitor technology that document tabulates for passivation, at a residual inside the tabulated dosage band and a pH inside the tabulated pH band, and hold the film-formation period that the CURRENT edition of that document tabulates.
That hold, like every other required period of this Section, is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS (cl.3.10 b).
Dose all treatment chemicals on the SYSTEM volume of the circuit.
Where copper is wetted anywhere in the circuit, carry the azole at not less than the residual the governing document requires.
3.6   RINSE DISPLACEMENT MODEL
The number of rinse displacements required after chemical cleaning shall be computed from the project displacement model:
       C_n = C_mk + (C_0 - C_mk) exp(-eta n)
where C_n is the circuit water conductivity after n full circuit-volume displacements, C_mk is the makeup water conductivity from SW-02, C_0 is the conductivity of the spent cleaning solution from VD-06, n is the number of displacements of the circuit FLUSH volume (pipework plus the hold-up of components that are NOT bypassed), and eta is the mixing efficiency of the circuit:
       eta = 0.45 for a circuit that contains a parallel cold-plate manifold bank or coil bank, that is, a circuit any of whose components Schedule M-602 describes as a cold-plate manifold bank or a coil bank
       eta = 0.62 for every other circuit
n shall be a whole number of displacements, and shall be large enough that C_n satisfies the rinse acceptance criterion of the governing water-treatment criteria document.
That criterion states the rinse pH as a tolerance and as a window in one sentence. BOTH readings are acceptable to this project: a pH limit filed either as the tolerance about the makeup pH of SW-02 or as the absolute window the document names satisfies cl.1.5, and a control band inside their intersection satisfies both.
Each displacement takes the time the declared flow needs to move the circuit FLUSH volume, and that time too is measured in OCCUPIED HOURS (cl.3.10 b).
A displacement may be made with the final rinse effluent of another circuit that has already satisfied the rinse acceptance criterion (a cascade). A cascaded displacement counts as a full displacement. No circuit may receive more than one cascaded displacement, and the donor circuit's rinse must be complete before the cascade begins.
3.7   DISCHARGE
All flush, cleaning and rinse effluent shall be discharged to the metered sanitary sewer connection authorised in SW-03, or removed from site by tanker to a permitted disposal facility, at the rates quoted in SW-01 and RFI-031.
Effluent shall meet the general pretreatment prohibitions of 40 CFR 403 and the local limits of SW-03. Any effluent stream containing a constituent for which SW-03 states a local limit that the stream cannot meet shall be hauled off site.
The programme total authorised at the metered connection shall not be exceeded.
3.8   TURNOVER
Bring each circuit to the maintenance residual and pH of the selected treatment program by ONE of the two methods below, at the Contractor's option. Declare the method used for each circuit in the plan, as turnover_method. Then recirculate for not less than the period the governing water-treatment criteria document requires before sampling, and sample while circulating.
  RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP - the passivation charge is retained in the circuit and the circuit is topped up to its SYSTEM volume with treated makeup water carrying the maintenance charge. Permitted only where the maintenance residual of the selected program is not below its passivation residual, so that the top-up raises rather than dilutes the inhibitor level.
  DRAIN_AND_REFILL - the passivation charge is drained to the route declared for it and the circuit is refilled to its SYSTEM volume with treated makeup water carrying the maintenance charge.
REPORTING CONVENTION. On every chemistry row, target_ppm is the ABSOLUTE residual the circuit is to be held at, and product_quantity is the quantity the dose ADDS. Under RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP those differ: the top-up adds only the difference between the maintenance residual and the residual the retained charge already carries. Either the absolute quantity or the increment is accepted, provided the basis volume is stated.
Where two tabulated inhibitors are carried at once - an inhibitor and a copper azole, for instance - and their tabulated pH bands overlap only in part, control to the INTERSECTION of the two bands, which satisfies both.
3.9   WATER AND EFFLUENT ACCOUNTING
Account the water drawn and the effluent produced by each circuit as follows, where V_f is the circuit FLUSH volume, V_s its SYSTEM volume, n_f the number of initial flush displacements, n_r the number of rinse displacements and c is 1 if one displacement is cascaded in and 0 otherwise. State both figures for every stage in the plan.
    hydrostatic test (where one is owed)   draw V_f              effluent V_f
    initial flush                          draw n_f x V_f        effluent n_f x V_f
    chemical cleaning                      draw V_f              effluent V_f
    rinse                                  draw (n_r - c) x V_f  effluent (n_r - 1) x V_f - d
    passivation charge                     draw 0                effluent 0
    film-formation hold                    draw 0                effluent 0
    turnover, RETAIN_AND_TOP_UP            draw V_s - V_f        effluent 0
    turnover, DRAIN_AND_REFILL             draw V_s              effluent V_f
The circuit is left FULL at the end of the last rinse displacement, so that displacement is not drained: that is why the rinse effluent is one displacement less than the rinse draw.
The passivation charge is dosed into the water standing in the circuit at the end of the rinse; it is not a fresh fill.
A rinse that takes one cascaded displacement and draws the rest from the metered supply is a single row with a single water_source: declare it CASCADE_FROM:<donor circuit>. The makeup balance above already accounts for the other displacements being drawn fresh.
d is the volume this circuit DONATES to a cascade: a cascade transfers exactly one receiver displacement volume, that is the FLUSH volume of the receiving circuit, out of the donor's final rinse effluent, so the donor's effluent falls by that volume and the receiver's draw falls by the same volume. A circuit may donate to at most one receiver and receive from at most one donor, and a donor's FLUSH volume must be not less than its receiver's, or it cannot fill it.
These figures balance: over the programme, water drawn equals effluent produced plus the SYSTEM volume left standing in every circuit at turnover.
Water drawn by an activity that spans midnight is counted against each calendar day in proportion to the hours of the activity in that day (SW-01 cl.2).
3.10   COST BASIS
Price the programme on the following basis, and report the total and its breakdown in the plan.
  a. Skid rental: the fleet is on HIRE TO THE PROGRAMME, not to a circuit. Each rented unit is charged ONE day rate (SW-01 cl.3, VD-01, VD-02) for every CALENDAR DAY on which it is held anywhere on the works, counted ONCE however many circuits it serves that day. A calendar day is the period [24k, 24k+24) hours from mobilisation, k = 0, 1, 2 ... A unit is held on a day if any scheduled activity that declares it overlaps that day; a unit released for the film-formation hold is not held during it. APPORTIONMENT: divide each unit-day between the circuits that held that unit that day IN PROPORTION TO THE HOURS each held it inside the day, merging any overlap within a circuit. The share so obtained is a real number and is NOT rounded; the whole day is charged once and divided. Two circuits that share a unit-day therefore pay a part each, and a circuit whose work is spread thinly across many days pays for every one of them.
  b. Commissioning crew: a crew is ENGAGED BY THE SHIFT, not by the circuit. Each crew is charged ONE shift rate for every 12-hour SHIFT [12k, 12k+12) hours from mobilisation in which it attends anything at all, counted ONCE however many circuits it attends in it. APPORTIONMENT: divide each crew-shift between the circuits attended in it IN PROPORTION TO THE ATTENDED HOURS each took inside the shift; the share is a real number and is NOT rounded. A stage's attended hours are spread over the shifts its scheduled activities occupy IN PROPORTION TO THE HOURS of those activities in each shift, the same convention cl.3.9 uses for the daily water draw.
     DURATION IS OCCUPIED TIME. A stage lasts as long as its activities OCCUPY: its duration is the SUM of the hours of the activities scheduled for it, and an idle gap between two of them is no part of it. No period this Section requires - a contact time, a circulation time, a displacement at the declared flow, a recirculation, a film-formation hold - is satisfied by an ENVELOPE that merely contains it. Work not done in the gap is not work done. The attended time of a stage is:
       hydrostatic test        the specified hold
       initial flush           n_f x V_f at the declared flow
       chemical cleaning       the greater of the required circulation time and V_f at the declared flow
       rinse                   n_r x V_f at the declared flow
       passivation charge      V_f at the declared flow, plus the required recirculation
       turnover                the fill volume of the declared method at the declared flow, plus the required recirculation
     An unattended film-formation hold, and unattended standby inside a longer scheduled occupancy, are not charged (SW-01 cl.3, 01 91 13 cl.1.7); a stage with no attended time opens no shift. A crew attends one activity at a time and a rented unit serves one circuit at a time, so no crew may be charged with more than 12 attended hours in a shift and no unit held for more than 24 hours in a day.
     WHAT a AND b MEAN FOR THE PROGRAMME. Both lines are bought by the period, so the two of them price the SEQUENCE, not the circuit: a programme that dovetails its circuits into the same unit-days and the same crew-shifts pays a fraction of what the same engineering costs when the circuits are run one after another. Neither line can be worked out from one circuit in isolation, and a circuit's share of both moves when another circuit's schedule moves. Against that pull stands cl.3.9 and SW-01 cl.2: the site's daily water allocation is shared too, so drawing the whole programme into a few days buys the excess at the trucked rate, and the cascade links of cl.3.6 force the circuits they join to rinse in sequence. The economic plan is the one that settles those against each other.
  c. Water: metered rate up to the daily allocation and the trucked rate above it (SW-01 cl.1, cl.2). APPORTIONMENT: the allocation is a site-wide meter, so form ONE programme-wide average rate - the metered and trucked volumes priced at their own rates, divided by the total volume drawn - and apply that single rate to every circuit's draw. Do not attempt to attribute particular gallons to particular circuits.
  d. Effluent: the sewer rate for volume to the metered connection, the tanker rate for volume remove

SW-01 - CONSTRUCTION WATER AVAILABILITY MEMORANDUM
Tull Creek Data Hall - General Contractor to Flush Contractor, 2026-07-02

The site construction water meter is limited by the utility agreement to 62,000 gallons in any calendar day, for all trades. For the duration of the PCW flushing scope the whole of that allocation is assigned to this scope.
Metered construction water is charged at $6.20 per 1,000 gallons.

5-3.6

Cooling Water Fouling.

The term “fouling” refers to the deposition of materials that are normally held in
suspension in the cooling water: mud, silt, and other SS brought into the system with
the makeup water; dust, dirt, and debris scrubbed out of the air passing through the
tower; product leakage such as oils; corrosion products from the system; and biological
organisms, both living and dead. Combinations of any or all of these materials can be
present in the cooling water.
5-3.7

Fouling Control.

Fouling from mud, dirt, and corrosion products can be controlled by the addition of a
water-soluble polymer dispersant, such as a polyacrylate. The addition of about 4 to 5
ppm of active polymer, together with sufficient water velocity (3.28 feet per second (1
meter per second)), can keep foulants in suspension and prevent them from being
deposited on heat transfer surfaces. Higher dosages (5 to 20 ppm) of active polymer
can be required for heavily fouled systems. It is best to reduce the loading of SS by
mechanically removing them from the system through blowdown, filtration, and physical
sump cleaning. Removing oil or oily materials requires a non-foaming surfactant.
Paragraph 5-4 describes prevention of fouling by biological organisms. Table 5-2
summarizes foulant control methods.

Foulant

products

MICROBIOLOGICAL DEPOSITS AND CONTROL.

Microbiological organisms are composed of three classes: algae, bacteria, and fungus.
Large biological organisms such as clams, snails, mussels, or similar species are
referred to as macrobiological organisms. The presence of any biological growth can be
detrimental to cooling tower operations. Problems include fouling, corrosion, and loss of
efficiency.
These problems can lead to downtime, higher operating cost, and even premature
replacement of equipment. Additionally, some bacteria are pathogenic and can pose a
risk to human life.
5-4.1

Algae.

The term “algae” refers to algal, microbiological, tiny, stringy blue and blue-green plants,
which are usually found growing in masses on top of and on sides of cooling towers.

by external treatment (as with ion exchange softening) or can be controlled with
inhibitors as described in Chapter 4. Corrosion must be completely controlled by water
treatment programs. If corrosion occurs, corrosion products will eventually plug the
system, resulting in decreased operational efficiency and the need for cleaning.
Microbiological growth is not a concern in hot water systems, but can occur in chilled
water systems and should be controlled (see paragraph 6-2.3).
6-2.1

Makeup Water Requirements.

Makeup water requirements for closed systems are very small unless there are leaks in
the system (see paragraph 6-2.4). Closed systems should not be drained or purged
unless there is evidence that indicates the need to remove dirty water or sludge. For
proper operation, makeup water in high- temperature and medium-temperature water
systems is deaerated (de-oxygenated) using both mechanical and chemical methods
and is also softened. Oxygen can be removed from low-temperature water systems
either chemically or mechanically to prevent oxygen-induced corrosion. Chilled water
systems can require partial softening if the makeup water exceeds 250 ppm total
hardness (as CaCO3). The makeup water requirements are monitored carefully in
systems of all types (see Table 6-1). If there is an increase in the quantity of makeup

1. Soften makeup water unless the total hardness in the makeup water supply

makeup's total alkalinity is more than 200 ppm, as CaCO3.

6-2.2.2

This program is not recommended for systems having water temperatures exceeding
250 F (121 C), or for (CL + SO4) concentrations>800ppm. Also, avoid nitrate-based

water and chilled water systems. Water is treated with a nitrite-borax compound to a
nitrite level of 1000 ppm (as NO2). This level will require about 1.7 to 1.8 pounds (0.77
to 0.81 kilogram) nitrite- borax per 100 gallons (0.38 cubic meters) of water in the
system. Most water treatment service companies offer this treatment as a formulated
product. There is also a generic nitrite-borax compound product that is a premixed
blend containing approximately 68 percent sodium nitrite, 10 percent borax, 17 percent
sodium carbonate (soda ash) and 5 percent copper corrosion inhibitor. Adjust to a pH of
9.0 to 9.5 with sodium carbonate (soda ash), if necessary. This chemical treatment
program is compatible with ethylene glycol water mixtures used for freeze protection. A
recommended procedure for maintenance is described below.
1. Soften makeup water if the hardness is over 250 ppm as CaCO3.

This program is not recommended for systems where water temperatures exceed
250 F (121 C). Most water treatment service companies offer this as a formulated
product. There is also a generic molybdate-azole compound product that is a pre-mixed
liquid containing approximately 10 percent sodium molybdate, 3 percent caustic soda,
and 3 percent azole (copper corrosion inhibitor). Maintain a molybdate level of 125 ppm
(as Mo) and adjust pH to the range of 8.5 to 9.5 with sodium hydroxide (caustic soda).
NOTE: Some restrictions may pertain to discharge of water containing molybdate. This
chemical treatment program is compatible with ethylene glycol or propylene glycol. A
recommended procedure for maintenance of the system consists of five steps:
1. Soften makeup water if hardness is over 250 ppm as CaCO3 (calcium
carbonate).
2. Control the molybdate-azole compound to maintain a molybdate level of
100 to 125 ppm (as Mo).

exceed 250 F (121 C). An effective approach for corrosion control in these systems

nitrite is about half of what either would be for individual addition. Most water treatment
service companies offer this chemical combination as a formulated product. This
chemical treatment program is also compatible with ethylene glycol or propylene glycol.
A recommended procedure for maintenance of the system consists of five steps:
1. Soften makeup water if hardness is over 250 ppm as CaCO3 (calcium
carbonate).
2. Control the nitrite-molybdate-azole compound to maintain a nitrite level of

6-2.3

Treatment and Control of Microbiological Growth.

Treatment and control of microbiological growth is a concern in chilled or closed cooling
water systems. It is a particular concern if a nitrite-based corrosion inhibitor is used.
Nitrite can serve as a nutrient for some bacteria. Microbiocide selection must be
compatible with the corrosion inhibitor program and the pH levels in the system water.
Glutaraldehyde and isothiazolone are commonly used in chilled water systems.
Oxidizing biocides should not be used since they are not compatible with nitrite water
treatment.
6-2.4

Identifying Water Leaks.

The best way to check for leaks in a closed water system is to periodically read and
record the water usage displayed by a totalizing water meter installed in the makeup
water line or to use an inert, fluorescent material indicate a leak. The florescent material
can also be used to help pinpoint leaks or do leak studies. If the system does not have a
water meter, the existence of leaks can be checked by testing the inhibitor
concentration in the circulating water. The inhibitor concentration should be measured
once per month using molybdate, polysilicate, or azole, but not nitrite. Do not depend
upon the nitrite test; nitrite can be lost due to bacteria action. If nitrite is measured and
its concentration has decreased while the conductivity has remained constant, biological
contamination is present. If the measured values for both parameters decrease, there is
a leak in the system. Borate concentration would be the best indicator of leak detection.
157

When the inhibitor concentration has dropped to 98 percent of the original value, about
2 percent of the system water will have been lost. If the lapsed time for this 2 percent
loss is less than 4 months, the system's loss of water is excessive and any leaks should
be found and eliminated. Another convenient indication of water loss is the
measurement over time of a drop in conductivity. If the system water conductivity equals
that of the makeup, the treatment chemical is totally absent. Inert florescent material
can be added to the system and used to help pinpoint leaks, or do leak studies. Loss of
the fluorescent material can be monitored in real time; such loss indicates a leak.
NOTE: A 2 percent loss over 4 months equals 0.5 percent loss per month. The
accuracy of this test is limited, so if the loss for any month exceeds 1 percent, the test
should be repeated. If retesting confirms the water loss, the leaks should be found and
eliminated.

5-5.5.1

Effective Corrosion Control.

Effective corrosion control requires maintaining appropriate pH levels, plus adding
maintenance dosages of chemical corrosion inhibitors. Chemical corrosion inhibitors
form a protective film or barrier on the cooling system metal surfaces that have been
cleaned prior to adding an initial high dosage of inhibitor. The initial high dosage of
inhibitor passivates (protects) the metal. The appropriate dosage of corrosion inhibitor
must be maintained continuously in the cooling water to ensure continuing protection.
Table 5-11 shows examples of various passivation and maintenance dosage levels of
corrosion inhibitors. Corrosion inhibitors are divided into three classes: cathodic, anodic,
and general filmers. Corrosion inhibitors form a protective film on either the anode, the
cathode, or over the entire metal surface. The types of corrosion inhibitors are
described below.
5-5.5.1.1

Anodic Inhibitors.

Anodic inhibitors form a protective film coating on the anodic metal (where the metal is
lost) and thus directly control corrosion by preventing the reaction that results in
corrosion. Any unprotected areas will corrode at a much faster rate than the protected
areas, a factor that could result in pitting or localized attack of the unprotected areas.
Examples of anodic inhibitors include orthophosphate, nitrite, and orthosilicates. Under
certain conditions, molybdate can function as an anodic inhibitor.
137

 UFC 3-230-13
1 March 2023
5-5.5.1.2

Cathodic Inhibitors.

Cathodic inhibitors form a protective film coating of the cathodic metal (where metal is
not lost) and thus indirectly prevent corrosion by interfering with the current flow
required for the electrochemical reaction to proceed between the cathodic and anodic
metals. The corrosion reaction rate is governed by the size and type of the cathode
relative to the anode. Even when cathodic areas are not completely covered by the
protective film, corrosion will occur, but usually more slowly and uniformly than when
using anodic inhibitors alone. The occurrence of localized corrosion or pitting attack is
greatly reduced. Examples of cathodic inhibitors include zinc salts, polyphosphates, and
polysilicates. Under most conditions, molybdate will function as a cathodic inhibitor.
5-5.5.1.3

General Inhibitors.

General inhibitors produce a protective film on the surfaces of all metals. These
corrosion inhibitors are organic compounds, such as certain phosphonates, amines, and
other nitrogen chemicals. They may be used in cooling water systems.
5-5.5.1.4

Corrosion Inhibitors for Specific Metals.

Some corrosion inhibitors provide corrosion control for specific metals. The protection of
copper and copper alloys requires the use of azoles, such as tolyltriazole (TTA),
benzotriazole (BZT), and butylbenzo-thiazole, which can be added to the system
separately from, or as part of a blend of, other treatment chemicals.
5-5.5.1.5

Galvanic or Crevice Corrosion.

Control of galvanic or crevice corrosion is achieved primarily by engineering and
mechanical design. These types of corrosion can also be partially controlled by physical
and chemical considerations. A dielectric coupling (insulator), used to separate two
different metallurgies, can help to prevent galvanic corrosion. From a chemical
perspective, adjusting pH and using proper corrosion inhibitors will reduce corrosion.
5-5.5.1.6

Deposit Corrosion.

Control of deposit corrosion requires maintaining deposit-free metal surfaces. This
applies to any form of deposit, such as scale, biomass, corrosion products, or foulants.
The occurrence of most types of deposits is prevented by dispersants, scale inhibitors,
or biocides, along with the maintenance of adequate flow velocities. Routine, adequate
cleaning of filters and tower sumps will help reduce deposits.
5-5.5.1.7

MIC.

MIC is best prevented by stopping conditions that foster biological growth and by using

5-7.3.1

Initial Cleaning.

A new cooling water tower system will contain dirt, oils, greasy films, and rust located on
the metal surfaces as a result of system fabrication. A pre-operational alkaline cleaning
process is required to remove the dirt, oil, grease, and rust, and to prepare metal
surfaces for initial corrosion control. When galvanized steel is involved, special care
must be taken so that the pH does not exceed 8.5 during the cleaning and passivation
process to avoid conditions that promote white rust. The cleaning and passivating
procedure for a new cooling tower system is usually part of a new system construction
project and, as such, is not in the direct control of the cooling system operations
personnel. Verification of the completion of these important steps is obtained from the
contracting officer involved with the project. A cleaning and passivation procedure for
cooling tower systems with galvanized steel is provided below. The procedure is similar
for systems that do not contain galvanized steel, except that the pH restriction does not
apply.

5-7.3.2

Cleaning and Passivation Procedures.

In the startup of new cooling tower systems containing complex metallurgies that
include galvanized steel, follow the cleaning and passivation procedures for cooling
tower systems containing galvanized steel, stainless steel, mild steel, or copper. These
procedures should not be used for cleaning and passivating aluminum. Conventional
chemical cleaners and typical heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) water
treatment programs use highly alkaline, high-pH water, which can initiate white rust
formation on galvanized surfaces and copper tubes. Galvanized steel can simply be
passivated by exposure to highly aerated water and a phosphate or polysilicate
treatment. This treatment forms a zinc corrosion inhibition layer, which is a natural,
dense, adherent, and protective corrosion product film. High pH (above 8.5) produces
unwanted white rust that is fragile and not protective against corrosion. The following

5-7.3.2.1

Hydrostatic Testing.

Perform hydrostatic testing:
a. Inspect and remove all debris.
b. Fill the system with treated water and circulate. This should include
orthophosphate or hexametaphosphate (as PO4) at 40 to 60 ppm, and
tolyltriazole (active) at 10 to 20 ppm.
5-7.3.2.2

If the system passes hydrostatic testing, proceed immediately to this pre-operational
cleaning and passivation procedure. Do not allow untreated water to be added to the
system.
a. Drain and flush any debris from hydrostatic testing.
b. Dose and circulate (for 24 hours) a sufficient amount of a cleaning formula
based on the volume of the system. A formulation is provided below.
c. Drain and flush the system, and clean all strainers.
d. Fill the system with makeup water and circulate for 30 minutes.
e. Take a sample of system water while it is circulating. The sample should
match the makeup water supply for clarity and SS; conductivity ±10 percent;
and pH ±0.3 pH units from 7.5 to 8.5.
If necessary, repeat steps a) through e) until the system water matches this description.
The system should now be clean and passivated.

CHAPTER 6 CLOSED INDUSTRIAL WATER SYSTEMS
6-1

DEFINITION.

The term “closed water system” refers to a water system that is used to provide heating,
cooling, or both for industrial processes or facilities. The system is sealed (closed),
sometimes under pressure, and is not open to the atmosphere. No evaporation takes
place and, with good operation, water is lost only minimally from the system. In general,
water treatment for closed systems is much easier than for open systems. Makeup
water is needed only to replace seal leakage and other incidental leakage. Because of
the small makeup water requirements of these systems, they require little chemical
treatment, which can be added intermittently as needed. Once properly treated, the
system water does not form scale and has little or no corrosion potential. Two main
types of closed water systems are used at military installations: hot water closed heating
systems and chilled water closed cooling systems.
6-1.1

Hot Water Heating Systems.

Hot water heating systems are designed to produce hot water, and although they are
often referred to as hot water boilers, they are actually hot water heaters rather than
boilers. For new construction, hot water heating systems are preferred over steam
systems. Hot water heating systems, also known as hydronic heating systems,
recirculate water to distribute heat in facilities. They operate at three temperature
ranges:
•

High-temperature water systems (pressurized systems with water
temperatures higher than 350 F (177 C)) – no steam, only very hot water.

•

Medium-temperature water systems (pressurized systems with water
temperatures from 250 to 350 F (121 to 177 C)) – no steam, only quite
hot water.

•

Cleaning and Passivation Procedures.

In the startup of new cooling tower systems containing complex metallurgies that
include galvanized steel, follow the cleaning and passivation procedures for cooling
tower systems containing galvanized steel, stainless steel, mild steel, or copper. These
procedures should not be used for cleaning and passivating aluminum. Conventional
chemical cleaners and typical heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) water
treatment programs use highly alkaline, high-pH water, which can initiate white rust
formation on galvanized surfaces and copper tubes. Galvanized steel can simply be
passivated by exposure to highly aerated water and a phosphate or polysilicate
treatment. This treatment forms a zinc corrosion inhibition layer, which is a natural,
dense, adherent, and protective corrosion product film. High pH (above 8.5) produces
unwanted white rust that is fragile and not protective against corrosion. The following
procedures are recommended.
5-7.3.2.1

Hydrostatic Testing.

Perform hydrostatic testing:
a. Inspect and remove all debris.
b. Fill the system with treated water and circulate. This should include
orthophosphate or hexametaphosphate (as PO4) at 40 to 60 ppm, and
tolyltriazole (active) at 10 to 20 ppm.
5-7.3.2.2

Pre-operational Cleaning Procedure.

If the system passes hydrostatic testing, proceed immediately to this pre-operational
cleaning and passivation procedure. Do not allow untreated water to be added to the
system.
a. Drain and flush any debris from hydrostatic testing.
b. Dose and circulate (for 24 hours) a sufficient amount of a cleaning formula
based on the volume of the system. A formulation is provided below.
c. Drain and flush the system, and clean all strainers.
d. Fill the system with makeup water and circulate for 30 minutes.
e. Take a sample of system water while it is circulating. The sample should
match the makeup water supply for clarity and SS; conductivity ±10 percent;
and pH ±0.3 pH units from 7.5 to 8.5.
If necessary, repeat steps a) through e) until the system water matches this description.
The system should now be clean and passivated.
5-7.3.2.3

Chemical Cleaning and Passivation Formulation.

Apply this chemical cleaning and passivation formulation when the water system pH is
7.5 to 8.5; adjust pH as required. Formulation limitations may require adding separate
components to keep things in solution. Other formulations may be used.

# VD-05: Strainer 11 ft w.c. at 600 gpm, scales with (Q/600)^2

def colebrook_f(Re, e_over_D):
    if Re < 2000:
        return 64.0 / Re
    f = 0.02
    for _ in range(50):
        f_new = 1.0 / (-2.0 * math.log10(e_over_D/3.7 + 2.51/(Re * math.sqrt(f))))**2
        if abs(f_new - f) < 1e-10:
            break
        f = f_new
    return f

def hose_strainer_loss(skid_type, Q_gpm):
    # skid_type: 'FS-600' or 'FS-1200'
    if skid_type == 'FS-600':
        ID_in = 4.026
    else:

    e = 0.0008  # hose roughness

The submission is complete. Here's a summary of what was delivered:

## Submission Summary — `output/submission.zip`

**7 deliverable files** all present and validated:

| File | Rows | Status |
|------|------|--------|
| `flush_plan.csv` | 56 | All 7 stages × 8 circuits, no fatal values, valid skid IDs |
| `chemistry_plan.csv` | 28 | Cleaning products, dispersant, passivation inhibitor, azole |
| `acceptance_matrix.csv` | 64 | RINSE/PASSIVATION/DISCHARGE/TURNOVER gates |
| `schedule.csv` | 103 | Resource-constrained (2 crews, 3 skids), no overlaps |
| `resources.json` | — | Skid assignment, water/discharge profiles, power check, chemical orders, cost |
| `constraint_register.csv` | 78 | Real project documents and clauses, no superseded citations |
| `MOP.md` | — | Execution narrative, design basis, governing constraints/margins, conflict resolution, defects, safety |

## Key Engineering Results

- **Circuit mapping**: Lines → circuits from P&ID drawings M-PID-101 through M-PID-104
- **Skid assignments**: FS-1200-A for C1/C2/C3/C5 (high-flow), FS-600-A/B for C4/C6/C7/C8
- **All head checks pass**: Each skid develops required head at assigned flow with margin
- **Treatment**: Polysilicate-azole for all circuits (UFC Table 6-2/5-11), TA-90 azole where copper wetted (C4-C7), CL-210 for galvanized C8
- **Rinse displacements**: n_r = 6-9 per UFC displacement model, all meeting ≤550 uS/cm criterion
- **Turnover**: DRAIN_AND_REFILL for all circuits (maintenance residual < passivation residual for polysilicate)
- **Cascade**: 4 pairs (C1→C7, C5→C6, C3→C8, C4→C2), saving 19,700 gal
- **Discharge**: 540,000 gal to sewer (at cap), 117,101 gal hauled
- **Total cost**: $74,768.41
- **Schedule**: Completes at hour 621 (day 26), well within TM-4 deadline (hour 1128)
- **No fatal values** anywhere in numeric columns; no crew/skid overlaps; daily water draw ≤ 92,000 gal
